title: _TRIAGE_SYSTEM was written fresh instead of derived from brief.SYSTEM_PROMPT
description:
Spec 5.2 requires the triage system prompt to be DERIVED from brief.SYSTEM_PROMPT and to name that symbol, so that triage and the brief share one view of what this project cares about. comprehend._TRIAGE_SYSTEM (comprehend.py:472-482) was written from scratch and names nothing.

This is divergence with teeth rather than a style point: the brief's own prompt wants crypto surfaced, and the triage domain list contains none. An item triage judges immaterial never reaches the knowledge base at all, so the two halves of the system can silently disagree about the domain while both look healthy. No test enforces the derivation.
design: NOT fixed inside the bqa.4b build, deliberately. The pre-registered gate in scripts/score_comprehension.py measures triage quality against THIS prompt; changing the prompt before the gate has ever run would mean the gate measures a different system from the one it was pre-registered against, which destroys the property that makes pre-registration worth anything. Sequence it the other way: run the gate, record the numbers, then change the prompt and re-measure.
acceptance_criteria: _TRIAGE_SYSTEM is derived from brief.SYSTEM_PROMPT and names the symbol, a test fails if the derivation is removed, and the change is made AFTER a baseline gate run so the before/after numbers are comparable.

title: An item with nothing to extract is retried three times as a failure
description:
_validate_item returns None both for a MALFORMED extraction row and for a well-formed row that legitimately contains nothing (spec 12.2 measured real stock-quote and market-summary junk in the corpus). run() cannot tell them apart, so an item with genuinely nothing in it is charged an integration attempt three times before the ceiling retires it, and is counted in failed_integration and gave_up_integration as though the model or the parser had failed.

Two costs. Three expensive integration calls per empty item. And the failure counters conflate 'the pipeline broke' with 'there was nothing here', which is the exact unattributable-count shape this project already has a rule against.

It concentrates on the sampled control arm by construction: sampled items are the ones BOTH triage halves rejected, so they are the most likely to contain nothing extractable. The pre-registered gate reads enum variance on the sampled arm against the topical arm, so an arm whose budget is spent on retries yields fewer assertions to compare.
design: Distinguishable without a prompt change: a row that parses cleanly but carries empty entities or events is 'valid but empty', while a row that fails a type or membership check is malformed. _validate_item currently collapses both to None. A sentinel for the first, plus a branch in run() that marks such an item integrated with nothing written rather than charging it an attempt, keeps the measurement honest -- a genuinely empty sample arm is a real finding about the sample, not a pipeline failure to hide.
acceptance_criteria: An item whose extraction is well-formed but empty is marked integrated exactly once, writes no rows, is not counted in failed_integration, and is never re-offered; a malformed row still charges an attempt. Both are pinned by tests.
close_reason: Fixed together (they both distort what the pre-registered comprehension gate measures). wvt: brief._post_messages gains keyword timeout/max_attempts defaulting to the signals budget, so that caller is provably unchanged (two positive-control tests). comprehend routes through a new _timed_post that logs each call's elapsed seconds, and sizes itself via two new settings knobs, COMPREHEND_INTEGRATE_TIMEOUT=300 and COMPREHEND_TRIAGE_TIMEOUT=90, plus compose anchors. Integration now makes ONE HTTP attempt: item_triage.integrate_attempts < 3 already retries across hourly passes, so a second HTTP attempt multiplied against it (up to 6 charged 8192-token generations per bad item) and spent DEADLINE_SECONDS, which the item-level retry does not. uer: _validate_item no longer collapses well-formed-but-empty into malformed; write_extraction marks such an item integrated, writes nothing, charges no attempt, and counts it in a new Tally.empty_extraction. Suite 1554 -> 1571 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped against live PG18; ruff clean. All four mutations caught (1/1/2/3 tests), and the two run()-level property tests assert the acceptance criterion (never re-offered) through the real integration SELECT rather than restating integrated_at, with a presence sibling proving a malformed row still comes back. NOT COMMITTED: awaiting approval per the conservative profile.

title: Re-integration accumulates events instead of superseding them
description:
Bumping INTEGRATE_PROMPT_VERSION makes comprehend.write_extraction re-extract an already-integrated item (correct, per spec 4.2). But a re-extraction takes the 'insert new event' branch and mints a fresh event_id, so assertions' ON CONFLICT (item_id, event_id) never fires and the item gains a SECOND event and assertion rather than replacing the first. Measured against a real database: 1 event / 1 assertion before a bump, 2 / 2 after.

Unreachable at v1 (INTEGRATE_PROMPT_VERSION never moves), so it did not hold the bqa.4b build. It matters the first time an operator bumps that knob: the affected events double rather than being replaced, inflating events and any corroboration figure read off them.

The spec claimed 'reprocessing cannot duplicate' and that was never enforced; corrected in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-04-comprehension-pipeline-design.md section 6 on 2026-09-05.
design: Not fixed inline because superseding needs a real design decision, not a patch. Constraints: this repo RETIRES rather than deletes (claims.retired_on, and the three FKs disagree about deletes), assertions carries FKs to events, and a superseded event may already be cited by another item's assertion. Options to weigh: (a) stamp events with the extraction that produced them and retire superseded ones; (b) give events a dedupe key, which is hard because summaries legitimately change between prompt versions -- that is the point of re-extracting; (c) accept accumulation and make the gate read only the newest extraction per item.
acceptance_criteria: A bumped INTEGRATE_PROMPT_VERSION leaves exactly one live event per extracted event, with the superseded one retired rather than deleted, and a test pins it by bumping the version and asserting the live count does not grow.

title: Fetch article text for material items: no outlet's RSS body carries it
description: MEASURED 2026-09-05, do not re-derive. No outlet in the corpus carries article text in items.body. capture.py stores entry.get('summary'), and 15 of 24 outlets have a median body under 150 chars. The two richest are CLAMPED, not long: SCMP min 487 max 503, OilPrice min 520 max 557 -- a server-side truncation signature, not natural variation. So fetching would be a genuine addition rather than a way of using what is already stored. Worse, the two HIGHEST-volume outlets have the least text because they are Google News proxies whose summary is the headline restated (Reuters: '...jail  Reuters'); with IranWire clamped at 140 that is 926 of 2270 items, 41 percent of volume, with no body beyond the title. SHAPE: fetch at INTEGRATION time for material items only (~10 percent of volume), reusing brief.fetch_web_source. NOT at capture time -- parent spec section 2 makes capture's cheapness governing, and a per-item fetch inside capture's 600s bound is how that bound breaks. GATE THIS ON EVIDENCE, not on the intuition that more text is better: bqa.4b's score_comprehension.py reports enum variance per body-depth tier precisely so we can see whether the 350+ tier actually extracts better than the sub-150 tier. If it does not, fetching buys nothing and this bead closes unbuilt.
acceptance_criteria: The per-depth-tier breakdown from scripts/score_comprehension.py shows the 350+ tier producing materially better enum variance than the sub-150 tier, OR this bead is closed unbuilt with that measurement recorded as the reason.

title: A vanished Postgres hangs the suite forever instead of failing it
description: Observed 2026-09-04: the Docker daemon died mid-run, taking the test Postgres with it. The suite did not fail - it HUNG, indefinitely, on the first DB-touching test of each file, and produced a handful of teardown errors on the way down that looked like test defects. Two causes compound. (1) db.is_configured() reads DATABASE_URL, so it answers 'configured' for a server that is gone; the skipif guard therefore does not fire and the tests run. (2) The clean_db/store/state_store fixtures call db.connect() with no connect_timeout, unlike the production read paths - brief._jobs_render and the supervisor both pass one - so libpq waits forever. The result is the worst diagnostic shape available: indistinguishable from a slow test, and it invites blaming whatever was edited most recently. Cost about 25 minutes of misattributed debugging. Fix: give the test fixtures the same bounded connect_timeout the production paths use, so a dead server is an immediate, named error.
acceptance_criteria: With DATABASE_URL pointing at a port nothing is listening on, the DB-backed tests fail within seconds naming the connection, rather than hanging. A test asserting exactly that, so the timeout cannot be dropped again silently.

title: Capture liveness is silent when capture_runs is empty
description: capture.liveness returns None when there are no capture_runs rows at all, so a deployment where the capture job never fires once is never alerted on. This is deliberate rather than an oversight: zero rows cannot distinguish 'freshly migrated, first fire not due yet' from 'the job is broken and has never started', and the two want opposite responses - an alert on the first would fire on every deploy and train the operator to ignore it. /capture renders the state plainly ('Capture has never run in this deployment') so it is visible on demand. The fix, if this ever bites, is a second signal the capture tables do not carry: job_runs already records every spawn from every entry path, so 'the scheduler has fired capture N times and capture_runs is still empty' is answerable and unambiguous, where the capture tables alone are not.
acceptance_criteria: A deployment where capture is scheduled but has never written a row is distinguishable from one where the first fire is not yet due, using job_runs rather than a guessed grace period.

title: The repo docker-compose.yml has drifted behind the host's: enrichment lines missing

Harmless on the running host - the importer only reads the environment while settings is empty, so neither name does anything there now - but it means the host copy and the repo copy disagree on one more line, and a rebuild from the host's file would reintroduce a variable nothing reads. tests/test_packaging.py now catches that class in the REPO; it cannot see the host's file, which is the gap this bead is about.

title: A permanently dead resident eventually goes quiet
description: Corrected during the final fix wave by reproduction: the reported defect (a dead commands daemon alerting every 5 minutes forever) does not happen. title: Build DATABASE_URL safely instead of splicing a password into a URI
description: POSTGRES_PASSWORD is spliced into DATABASE_URL by plain docker-compose substitution with no encoding. Verified against libpq: + = ? : and # are safe, but / and % are parse errors and @ truncates the password and corrupts the host. openssl rand -base64 24 draws from A-Za-z0-9+/= so roughly 40 percent of generated passwords contain a / and break the stack. A dollar sign is separately eaten by compose interpolation unless written twice, and because it truncates identically on both DATABASE_URL and the postgres service's own password the stack comes up and WORKS with a shorter password than the operator wrote - the one genuinely silent case. Phase 1 ships prescriptive documentation (use openssl rand -hex 32) as the pragmatic fix. The durable fix is to stop hand-building a URI: either have db.connect fall back to discrete PG variables when DATABASE_URL is unset, or build the conninfo with psycopg.conninfo.make_conninfo which escapes properly. Rejected for now: hand-built keyword strings, which only narrow the character class and still break on a space or a quote.
close_reason: Compose passes the discrete POSTGRES_* variables through and db.conninfo builds the libpq string with psycopg make_conninfo; DATABASE_URL is now the explicit external-database escape hatch. Verified against a real postgres with password a/b@c%cd$e configured only through the discrete vars: 41 DB tests passed none skipped, and the old spliced URI fails on the same server. Commit 27aee22.

title: Add POSTGRES_USER/PASSWORD/DB to .env.example
description: The cutover added three required compose variables. POSTGRES_PASSWORD is :?-required, so an operator following the documented cp .env.example .env gets a hard compose failure naming the missing variable rather than silence - acceptable, but the example file should carry them. Not done during the cutover because .env.example is outside the agent tool scope (a guard blocks .env paths); the operator or a session with access should add POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD and POSTGRES_DB with safe placeholder values. Also worth confirming DATABASE_URL needs no entry there, since compose derives it from those three.
design: Premise correction (2026-09-01, with 0q0.11): DATABASE_URL is no longer DERIVED from the POSTGRES_* trio -- compose now defaults it to empty and passes POSTGRES_HOST/PORT/USER/PASSWORD/DB through as themselves. So the answer to this bead's open question is: .env.example needs no live DATABASE_URL entry, but it should carry a commented one explaining it is the outside-the-stack escape hatch. The block to paste is in --notes. Still blocked for agents: .env paths are denied to both the Bash and Read tools, so an operator has to paste it.
notes:
# --- Postgres: the supervisor's run ledger, advisory locks and scheduler state ---
# Required. The stack refuses to start without it rather than bringing up an
# unauthenticated database. Generate it with:  openssl rand -hex 32
# Avoid `$`: compose interpolation eats it unless you write `$$`, and it truncates
# identically on the app AND on the database, so the stack comes up and works with
# a shorter password than you wrote. `/ % @` are safe -- the app builds a libpq
# keyword/value conninfo, not a URI.
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=replace-me-with-openssl-rand-hex-32
POSTGRES_USER=newsbrief
POSTGRES_DB=newsbrief

# Optional; these are the compose defaults, shown for reference.
#POSTGRES_HOST=postgres
#POSTGRES_PORT=5432

# Optional. A full libpq URI for a database OUTSIDE this stack. When non-empty it
# wins over the POSTGRES_* variables above. It is a URI, so percent-encode the
# password inside it. POSTGRES_PASSWORD stays required even then: the bundled
# postgres service still starts and still demands one.
#DATABASE_URL=

Could not be done by an agent: .env* paths are denied to both the Bash and the Read tool, re-probed 2026-09-01 rather than assumed, so the paste-ready block was handed over instead. Contents not verified by me - I cannot read the file; the operator confirmed the paste. Open question in the original description is answered in the design field: DATABASE_URL needs no live entry, only a commented one, since compose passes POSTGRES_HOST/PORT/USER/PASSWORD/DB through as themselves rather than deriving a URI (0q0.11, 27aee22).

title: Ledger storage now grows without bound: non-standing claims never retire
description: news-brief-jx9.6 exempted broken and challenged claims from the TTL, deliberately and correctly - a broken claim is the accountability record and must outlive the window. The consequence is that brief_memory.json now has no upper bound in TIME for non-standing rows, only for standing ones. Storage was already unbounded in COUNT since j07, but the TTL bounded it in time; that bound is now gone for exactly the rows that accumulate permanently. The file is loaded and rewritten on every run, so this is real but slow. Not urgent: at roughly 0.27 breaks per brief measured in the replay, it is on the order of 100 rows a year. Revisit when the KB epics move storage off JSON, or sooner if the file gets slow to parse. Whatever is done must NOT delete the accountability record - archiving resolved rows out of the hot file is the shape of the fix, not eviction.
